links.note: 464 says those who fear disgrace do not begin what is not clear to them (தெளிவு இலதனைத் தொடங்கார்). 491 gives the same ban on beginning (தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும்) a concrete test: until the place has been seen (இடங்கண்ட பின் அல்லது). Read together, knowing the ground is one specific form of the clarity 464 demands before any start.

Parimelazhagar reads 491's முற்றும் இடம் as a place from which the enemy can be encircled, and tells the king neither to act nor to scorn the foe before finding one. 747 defines a fort from the other side as what cannot be taken even by encircling (முற்றியும் ... பற்றற்கு அரியது). The shared siege verb shows attacker and defender reasoning about the same ground; Manakkudavar instead reads 491 as 'the place where the task can be completed', which would loosen this link.

492 says that even for those with fighting strength (முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பினவர்க்கும்) the advantage of joining a fort (அரண்சேர்ந்தாம் ஆக்கம்) yields many gains. 741 says a fort is of value to those able to go on the offensive (ஆற்றுபவர்க்கும்) as well as to those who guard themselves in fear. Both deny that a fort is only for the weak: the chapter on place and the chapter on forts make the same point about the strong.

493 says even those without strength win (ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப) if they know the place and act against foes while guarding themselves (போற்றிச் செயின்). 878 says the enemy's pride dies when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (வகையறிந்து தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Self-guarding plus knowledge is the common recipe; 878 generalises 493's 'place' to knowing the way of acting.

861 advises avoiding opposition to the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and pursuing enmity against the weaker. 493 says the weaker side can still become strong and win when it knows the ground and protects itself. 493 therefore sets a condition under which 861's rule about relative strength does not settle the outcome.

494 says those who had planned (against you) lose their plan (எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர்) when you advance knowing the place and hold close to it. 440 says the enemies' scheme becomes void (ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்) when a ruler enjoys what he loves without letting the love be known. In both, the opponent's design is defeated before any fight by removing what it relied on: bad ground in one case, a known weakness in the other.

495: the crocodile wins in deep water (நெடும்புனலுள் வெல்லும் முதலை) and is killed by others once it leaves it. 481: the crow beats the owl by day (பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை), so kings need the right moment. The two adjacent chapters open their argument with the same kind of animal proof, one showing that strength depends on time and the other that it depends on place.

495 shows a strong animal losing outside its own element: the crocodile out of water is killed by others. 500 gives the sharper case, where a jackal kills a fearless war elephant in mud where its feet sink (காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும்). Together they state both halves: one's own ground makes one win, and the wrong ground lets even a much weaker creature win.

496 says chariots with strong wheels do not run on the sea and sea-going ships do not run on land (கடலோடா ... நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து); Manakkudavar takes it to mean that instruments must be made to suit the place. 675 lists means and place together (கருவி ... இடனொடு ஐந்தும்) among the five things to think through before acting. 496 shows why the two items in 675's list cannot be weighed separately: a tool is only a tool in its own medium.

497 says that one who thinks everything through and acts by the place needs no support but fearlessness (அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா). 534 says the fearful have no fortress (அச்சமுடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை): Parimelazhagar explains that forest or hill forts are of no use to a frightened mind. The pair shows the two sides of one claim: place is enough given courage, and place is worthless without it.

497 says no ally is needed (துணைவேண்டா) beyond fearlessness when the plan is complete and the ground right. 875 advises one who has no ally and two enemies (தன்துணை இன்றால் பகையிரண்டால்) to make one of the enemies a pleasing ally. 875 shows that the book does not treat being without allies as generally safe; 497's claim holds only under its stated condition of complete planning and the right place.

498 says the drive of a commander with a large army is destroyed (உறுபடையான் ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்) if he enters ground suited to a small army. 744 defines a fort as having little to guard and much room, and as destroying the drive of the foe who comes against it (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்பது அரண்). The shared phrase shows that a fort is the built form of 498's principle: ground chosen so that numbers stop counting.

473 says many who did not know their own strength pressed on out of zeal and broke midway (ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார்). 498 says the large army's zeal (ஊக்கம்) is destroyed when it enters the small army's ground. In both, drive that outruns a sober measure, of one's strength in one chapter and of the ground in the other, is what gets broken.

495 gives the image: the crocodile wins in its own deep water. 499 states the human case without an image: even people with no fortress and no great standing (சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும்) are hard to engage on the land where they live (உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது). 499 applies the crocodile's lesson to an invader's estimate of a weak-looking people.

500: a jackal kills, in sinking mud, an elephant that is fearless and faces spearmen (கண்ணஞ்சா வேலாள் முகத்த களிறு). 599: an elephant, though huge and sharp-tusked, fears when a tiger attacks (வெரூஉம் புலிதாக்குறின்). Both use the elephant to show that bulk and weapons do not decide a fight; 599 locates the missing factor in inner drive, 500 in the ground underfoot.

501 names four tests, virtue, wealth, pleasure and fear for life (அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம்), by which a person is examined before being trusted (தேறப்படும்). 513 names four qualities, love, understanding, clarity and freedom from desire, in whoever has which trust lies (நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு). The first four are trials applied from outside (Parimelazhagar describes staged temptations); the second four are the traits such trials are meant to find.

501 presents the fourfold examination as the way a person comes to be trusted. 514 says that even when trusted after every kind of test (எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும்), many people turn different through the nature of the work (வினைவகையான் வேறாகும்). The next chapter thus limits what 501's tests can guarantee: they show the person before office, not in it.

501's fourth test is fear for one's life (உயிரச்சம்). 690 defines the envoy as one who, even if it brings his end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்), does not fall short in securing his lord's good. The envoy chapter shows what passing that fourth test looks like in service.

502 places trust in one born of good family, free of faults, with a shame that recoils from blemish (குடிப்பிறந்து ... வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). 794 says the friendship of one born of good family who is ashamed of blame on himself (குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவானை) should be had even at a price. The same two criteria, birth and shame, are used to choose a king's officer and to choose a friend.

502 lists good family first and shame last among the grounds for trust. 951 says integrity and shame are found together by nature (இயல்பாகச் செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு) only in those born to a good house. 951 supplies the reasoning 502 leaves unstated: family is asked for because it is taken to be where shame comes naturally.

502 makes birth in a good family (குடிப்பிறந்து) a ground for trust alongside freedom from fault. 133 says having good conduct is itself good birth, and a lapse in conduct becomes low birth (ஒழுக்கம் உடைமை குடிமை இழுக்கம் இழிந்த பிறப்பாய் விடும்). On 133's definition, 502's first criterion cannot be checked apart from its second: family does not vouch for a person whose conduct fails.

503 observes that even in those who have learned hard things and are free of fault, it is rare on examination to find no blankness (இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு). 504 gives the rule that follows: examine the qualities and the faults and judge by what predominates (மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்). Parimelazhagar on 504 makes the bridge explicit, saying no one in the world has only qualities or only faults.

503 says hard learning and freedom from fault still leave some ignorance when one looks closely. 373 says that however many subtle books one studies, one's own inherent understanding still prevails (தன் உண்மை அறிவே மிகும்). Both set a limit on what study can change in a person, one in the chapter on choosing officers and one in the chapter on fate.

504 tells the king to examine a person's qualities and faults (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி) and take whichever predominates. 793 tells one to know a person's qualities, family, faults and kin (குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் ... இனனும்) before forming a friendship. The same inventory is used in both domains, but only 504 says how to decide when the inventory is mixed.

504 judges another person by the balance of qualities over faults. 433 says those ashamed of blame treat a fault of their own as small as a millet seed as if it were the size of a palmyra (தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம் ... பனைத்துணையாக் கொள்வர்). The book uses a weighing standard for assessing others and a much stricter one for oneself; the pair marks where 504's tolerance stops.

504 lets the predominant side decide what a person is. 965 says even those like a hill are diminished if they do a lowering thing the size of a kundri seed (குன்றி அனைய செயின்). 965 names a kind of fault, the degrading act, that is not outweighed by the mass of a person's merits, which limits the simple weighing of 504.

505 says a person's own deeds are the touchstone (கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்) of greatness and smallness. 986 asks what the touchstone of worth is (சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின்) and answers: accepting defeat even from those not one's equal. Both use the assayer's stone for testing people; 505 names the general test, deeds, and 986 picks one particular deed as the decisive one.

505 makes deeds the test of greatness and smallness. 279, on false ascetics, says the straight arrow is cruel and the bent lute is sweet, so people are to be taken by the nature of their deeds (வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்). The same test, deeds over appearance or standing, is used for judging renouncers in Book 1 and candidates for office in Book 2.

505 says greatness and smallness are assayed by each person's own deeds (தத்தம் கருமமே). 972 says birth is alike for all living beings and distinction differs through the difference in the work they do (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமையான்). 972 gives the wider ground for 505's test: if birth does not differentiate, deeds are the only thing left to examine.

502 puts trust in one who has a shame that recoils from blemish (நாணுடையான்). 506 warns against trusting those who are cut off (அற்றார்), because they have no attachment and are not ashamed of blame (பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி); Parimelazhagar takes அற்றார் as those without kin, Manakkudavar as those without conduct. The two verses are the positive and negative of one criterion, and 506 adds a cause: shame depends on having ties.

506 treats having no attachment (பற்றிலர்) as a reason not to trust a person, since such a one does not fear blame. 350 tells the renouncer to hold to the one without attachment (பற்றற்றான்) in order to let attachment go. The same word is a disqualification in the chapter on choosing officers and the goal in the chapter on renunciation; the contexts differ, so this is a contrast of valuation across the books and not a contradiction.

507 says trusting the ignorant with affection as the ground (காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்) yields every kind of folly. 515 says work is not to be assigned to someone because he is dear (சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற்றன்று), only to one who knows, endures and can do it. Both exclude affection as a ground of appointment, one at the stage of trust and the other at the stage of assigning work.

507 warns that trusting those without understanding out of fondness brings all folly on the one who trusts. 836 describes the result from the other side: when a fool who does not know how takes up a task (கையறியாப் பேதை வினைமேற் கொளின்), it fails and he ends in fetters. 836 shows the outcome that 507's warning anticipates.

508: one who trusts an outsider without examining (தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான்) gets trouble that does not end, extending to his descendants (வழிமுறை தீரா இடும்பை). 792: the friendship of one who does not inquire again and again ends in a grief that kills him (கடைமுறை தான்சாம் துயரம்). The same structure, unexamined acceptance followed by lasting harm, is stated for a king's officer and for a friend.

508 and 510 share their closing line (தீரா இடும்பை தரும்) and their first fault, trusting without examining. 510 adds a second fault of equal weight: doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்). Read after 508, 510 shows that the chapter's warning is not simply 'trust less': misplaced doubt is punished in the same words as misplaced trust.

509 says trust no one without examining, and after examining, trust what is to be trusted (தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்). 518 says that after examining a person's fitness for the work (வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை), make him fully entitled to it (அதற்குரியனாகச் செயல்). 518 turns 509's second half into an act: the trust that follows examination is shown by handing over real authority.

509 orders examination first and commitment after. 791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, because for those who keep friendship there is no letting go once it is made (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). Friendship follows the same sequence as appointment, and 791 states the reason the order matters: the commitment is hard to reverse.

509 says that once a person has been examined, what is to be trusted should be trusted. 588 says even what a spy has found and brought back should be checked through another spy (மற்றுமோர் ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்). For intelligence reports the book keeps verifying after the agent is chosen, which bears on 509's phrase தேறும் பொருள்: Manakkudavar reads it as the matters in which the person is reliable, not everything.

510 says doubting one who has been trusted (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. 519 says fortune leaves the one who thinks otherwise of the closeness of a man devoted to his work (கேண்மை வேறாக நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு). Both make the ruler's unfounded suspicion of a proven servant a cause of his own loss.

510 forbids doubting a person once trusted. 520 tells the king to look into things daily (நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன்), because the world stays straight only if the one doing the work stays straight. On a strict reading of 510 daily scrutiny looks like the doubt it forbids; read together, the book separates routine oversight of the work from suspicion of the person.

510 speaks to the ruler: doubt of one already trusted brings trouble that does not end. 693 speaks to the courtier: guard against grave faults, because once suspicion has arisen it is hard for anyone to clear it (கடுத்தபின் தேற்றுதல் யார்க்கும் அரிது). The two verses describe the same event, a ruler's suspicion, as lasting damage from each side of the relationship.
